stories.headline: Russian Drone Strikes Romanian Apartment Building, Injuring Two; Romania Expels Russian Consul
stories.summary:
A Russian drone, part of an overnight attack on Ukraine, crashed into an apartment building in eastern Romania early Friday, injuring two people. Romanian authorities said the drone was likely struck by Ukrainian air defenses over Ukrainian territory before altering its trajectory and crossing into NATO member Romania. Romanian President Nicusor Dan announced the expulsion of the Russian consul in the city of Constanta in response to the incident.

The Kremlin confirmed President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the incident. Former Russian Security Council deputy chairman Dmitry Medvedev warned Europe to brace for more such incidents, arguing that European weapons and intelligence are used daily in strikes on Russian territory. The Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would respond swiftly to Romania's decision to close the Russian consulate in Constanta.

The incident marks one of the most direct intrusions into NATO territory linked to the Ukraine war and raises urgent questions about escalation risk within the alliance. Romania is a NATO member, and the strike on civilian infrastructure — however inadvertent — puts the alliance's Article 5 mutual defense commitments under scrutiny. Western officials have not yet formally characterized the incident as a NATO matter.

The development comes as Russia remains broadly at a standstill on the ground in Ukraine, with assessments showing minimal territorial changes in 2026. The drone incident underscores the widening geographic footprint of the conflict and the risks of spillover into neighboring countries, particularly those bordering the active war zone.

stories.headline: Israel Added to UN Sexual Violence Blacklist for First Time; Israel Severs Ties with UN Secretary General's Office
stories.summary:
The United Nations placed Israel on its annual blacklist of parties that commit conflict-related sexual violence for the first time Friday, in a report released by the office of Secretary General António Guterres. The report said UN investigators had verified 31 cases of sexual violence perpetrated by Israeli military, police, and prison service personnel against Palestinians from Gaza and the West Bank — 18 cases from prior years and 13 occurring in 2025. Verified violations included rape, gang rape, forced nudity, and violence to genitals against 14 men, seven women, nine boys, and one girl.

Israel responded forcefully, rejecting the allegations and announcing it would sever relations with Guterres's office for as long as he leads the UN. Israeli Ambassador to the UN Danny Danon accused Guterres of spreading antisemitic lies. Israel said its attempts to be heard were obstructed and that its forces operate fully within the law.

The same report noted that Hamas was previously added to the list, and that 12 former hostages released from Gaza had made allegations of sexual violence against Hamas captors — allegations the UN said it could not verify because Israel denied UN bodies access to conduct investigations. Critics of Israel say the pattern of allegations, including a high-profile leaked CCTV footage case at the Sde Teiman detention facility, suggests systemic abuse; supporters of Israel argue the UN process is politically motivated and lacks evidentiary rigor.

The listing carries significant diplomatic weight and adds to international pressure on Israel at a moment when it is simultaneously engaged in military operations in Gaza and southern Lebanon. The UN Committee against Torture said last November it was deeply concerned about reports indicating a de facto state policy of organized and widespread torture of Palestinian detainees.

stories.headline: ICE Agent Arrested in Texas for January Minneapolis Shooting of Venezuelan Man
stories.summary:
Federal and state law enforcement arrested a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer in Texas on Friday in connection with a nonfatal shooting that occurred during a January immigration sweep in Minneapolis. Christian Castro was taken into custody by agents from the Department of Homeland Security's Office of the Inspector General and the Texas Rangers, 11 days after Minneapolis prosecutors charged him with assault and falsely reporting a crime.

The shooting took place on January 14 during Operation Metro Surge, when Castro allegedly shot a Venezuelan man, Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis. Video evidence that emerged after the incident contradicted Castro's official account, leading to the criminal charges. Castro had apparently left Minnesota and was located in Texas before his arrest Friday.

The arrest is notable as a rare instance of a federal immigration enforcement officer facing criminal prosecution for conduct during an immigration operation, at a time when the Trump administration has dramatically expanded enforcement activity. Supporters of aggressive immigration enforcement have argued officers face dangerous conditions in the field and deserve broad legal protection; critics contend the case illustrates a lack of accountability within federal immigration agencies.

The case intersects with broader tensions around immigration enforcement, including ongoing protests at the Delaney Hall detention facility in Newark, New Jersey, where clashes between demonstrators and federal agents have escalated in recent days. The arrest comes as the Justice Department has simultaneously filed suit against four Democratic-led states over policies it says endanger ICE agents.

stories.headline: First Survivor Evacuated from Laos Cave After More Than a Week Trapped by Floodwaters
stories.summary:
Rescue divers in Laos successfully evacuated the first of five villagers trapped in a flooded cave in Xaisomboun province late Friday, after the group had been stranded underground for more than a week. The evacuated man was seen walking unsteadily with the assistance of two rescuers before being handed over to medical personnel. Evacuations of the four remaining survivors were suspended until Saturday as rescuers assessed their readiness and dealt with complications from a morning rainstorm.

The five villagers were discovered alive on Wednesday by divers who found them sitting on a rock in the darkness of the cave. Two additional people who entered the cave with the group remain missing. Lao and Thai rescue teams have been working to pump floodwater from the cave's passages while supplying the trapped men with water, soft food, and foil blankets.

The villagers reportedly entered the cave to search for valuable minerals before flash flooding cut off their exit. One member of the group escaped in time and alerted authorities to those left behind. Video recorded inside the cave on Thursday showed the desperate conditions the men were enduring after days of waiting in darkness.

The rescue operation drew significant international attention and involved coordination between Lao and Thai volunteer rescue organizations. The incident drew comparisons to past high-profile cave rescues in Southeast Asia, most notably the 2018 rescue of a youth soccer team from a flooded cave in Thailand.

stories.headline: U.S. Designates Brazil's Two Largest Drug Gangs as Foreign Terrorist Organizations
stories.summary:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced Thursday that the First Command of the Capital (PCC) and the Red Command (CV) — Brazil's two largest criminal organizations — will be formally designated as foreign terrorist organizations effective June 5. In the interim, both groups have been named specially designated global terrorists, restricting their ability to conduct financial transactions. The two gangs are estimated to have more than 50,000 members combined, with operations centered in São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro and networks extending across South America and into Europe.

The announcement came one day after a visit to Washington by Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro and a presidential candidate who has advocated for the designation. Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has repeatedly stated he would view such a move as U.S. interference in Brazil's domestic politics ahead of October's presidential election, in which Flávio Bolsonaro is a potential rival. Lula had not commented on Thursday's announcement as of publication.

Rubio framed the action as part of the Trump administration's broader regional counter-narcotics strategy, which has included designating eight Latin American cartels as foreign terrorist organizations and conducting military boat strikes against suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. 'Their influence and illicit networks extend far beyond Brazil's borders, across our region and into our country,' Rubio said.

The designation carries significant diplomatic weight, potentially straining relations with Brazil — South America's largest nation and a major U.S. trading partner — at a sensitive political moment. Critics argue the timing, coinciding with Bolsonaro's Washington visit, lends credence to Lula's claims of electoral interference, while supporters contend the criminal organizations pose a genuine transnational threat warranting the action.

stories.headline: Update: Swiss Islamist Terror Suspect Stabs Three at Winterthur Train Station Days After Psychiatric Release
stories.summary:
A 31-year-old Swiss man stabbed three people at the Winterthur train station in Switzerland on Friday morning, injuring a 28-year-old, a 43-year-old, and a 52-year-old, all Swiss nationals. The 52-year-old sustained a stab wound to the thigh and underwent emergency surgery, while the other two victims received wounds to the leg and neck. The suspect was arrested at the scene.

Zurich cantonal police commander Marius Weyermann said the suspect had come to authorities' attention in 2015 for distributing Islamic State propaganda. On Monday of this week, the man was taken to a psychiatric hospital after presenting himself at a police station making incoherent statements. He was discharged Tuesday, returned by officers, and then certified by doctors on Wednesday as no longer posing a danger — one day before the attack. Eyewitnesses reported hearing the attacker shout 'Allahu Akbar' before striking victims with a knife.

Swiss President Guy Parmelin called the incident a 'terrorist attack' on social media, and Canton Zurich's security director Mario Fehr said it was 'clear from the scene that the motive for this act must be sought in the realm of radicalisation and extremism.' A school teacher was reported to have stood in front of a group of passing schoolchildren to shield them during the attack.

This is a new development on a previously noted story: earlier reporting flagged an Islamist suspect's stabbing at a Swiss station. Today's update confirms the suspect's psychiatric history, the timeline of his release just 48 hours before the attack, and official terrorism designation by Swiss authorities — raising urgent questions about the decision to discharge him.

stories.headline: Update: Jill Biden's Stroke Fear Admission Draws Bipartisan Criticism Over Democratic Concealment of Biden's Health
stories.summary:
Former First Lady Jill Biden told CBS News in a pre-publication interview that during the June 2024 presidential debate she thought former President Joe Biden was having a stroke, saying 'I thought, Oh my God, he's having a stroke, and it scared me to death.' The admission, tied to the release of her new memoir, contradicts the posture adopted by both the former first lady and the broader Biden political operation in the immediate aftermath of the debate, when they publicly defended the president's performance and vigorously attacked media reports questioning his cognitive fitness.

The disclosure has drawn criticism from across the political spectrum. CNN anchor Abby Phillip called out the 'deceptiveness that was behind this,' asking on air, 'What kind of political system covers that up? And makes it OK to lie to people about what everybody knows is true?' Phillip also noted that The Wall Street Journal had published reporting on Biden's health at the time and was 'attacked viciously by the White House.' Conservative commentators and the current White House have demanded accountability for what they describe as a deliberate cover-up.

The White House said Jill Biden 'should have to answer' for the concealment of the former president's decline. Podcast host Kmele Foster, appearing on CNN, argued the central unanswered question remains why she publicly defended her husband's performance at the time if she privately feared he was having a stroke. The debate ultimately triggered a chain of events that led Biden to withdraw from the 2024 race in favor of Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost the general election to Donald Trump.

The story reignites debate over the degree to which Democratic Party leadership was aware of Biden's condition and chose to suppress it from public view. Supporters of the Biden family argue Jill Biden's candor in the memoir represents a form of accountability, while critics on both the right and within the Democratic Party contend the admission underscores a serious breach of transparency with voters.

stories.headline: Three Latvian Climbers Killed in Fall on Alaska's Mount McKinley; One Rescued
stories.summary:
Three members of a Latvian mountaineering expedition died after falling near Denali Pass on Alaska's Mount McKinley, the highest peak in North America, a Latvian mountaineering group confirmed Friday. A fourth climber from the group was rescued by Denali National Park and Preserve search and rescue personnel late Thursday. The fall occurred Wednesday at approximately 18,200 feet on the West Buttress route, the mountain's most popular path to the summit.

The four climbers were part of a seven-person Latvian team when the accident occurred on a section of the route known for its crevasses, steep ice, and exposed ridges. Park rangers noted that the stretch between high camp at 17,200 feet and Denali Pass has been the site of numerous injuries and deaths over the years, most caused by unprotected falls. The remaining three team members tended to those who fell before retreating to camp.

More than 130 people have died on Mount McKinley throughout the park's history, and only about 1,000 to 1,200 climbers attempt the summit annually. As of Thursday, 516 climbers were on the mountain. Last year, the peak recorded two fatalities. The deaths mark a significant casualty event for a single expedition on the mountain.

stories.headline: Shangri-La Dialogue Opens With China's Military Rise and Indo-Pacific Tensions in Focus
stories.summary:
Asia's premier annual defense summit, the Shangri-La Dialogue, opened Friday in Singapore with Vietnam's President To Lam delivering the keynote address to an audience that included U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and a high-level Chinese military delegation. Lam warned that the ongoing conflict in the Middle East — and Iran's stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz — had demonstrated how a single regional flashpoint can cascade into global economic disruption, drawing an implicit lesson for the South China Sea and broader Indo-Pacific.

Lam called on both the United States and China to abide by international law to prevent a global crisis, a message aimed at managing competing maritime claims in the region. Vietnam has unresolved territorial disputes with Beijing in the South China Sea but remains heavily dependent on China economically, placing it in a delicate position between the two superpowers.

Hegseth is scheduled to open Saturday's session with a speech focused on the Trump administration's Indo-Pacific strategy. His attendance signals continued U.S. engagement in the region despite attention focused on the Middle East ceasefire and the ongoing Ukraine war, both of which also featured in discussions at the summit.

The conference comes at a particularly fraught moment, with China's military modernization advancing rapidly and U.S. alliances in the region undergoing stress tests. The forum brings together defense ministers and military chiefs from dozens of nations and is considered a key venue for signaling strategic intentions in the Pacific.

stories.headline: JFK Airport Begins Enhanced Ebola Screening for Travelers From Outbreak Nations
stories.summary:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced Thursday that John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York City will conduct enhanced Ebola screenings for passengers arriving from countries affected by the ongoing Central and East African outbreak, effective 11:59 p.m. Thursday. The move expands existing screening infrastructure to one of the world's busiest international transit hubs as the outbreak continues to outpace the global response.

The Congo outbreak involves a less common strain of Ebola virus for which no specific treatments or approved vaccines are currently available, complicating containment efforts. World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus traveled to the region to underscore international support, telling reporters that the visit was intended to signal to affected communities 'that they're not alone.'

The JFK screening expansion reflects growing concern among U.S. public health officials about the virus reaching American shores via international travel. The U.S. previously announced broader travel screening measures in coordination with Mexico and Canada ahead of the 2026 World Cup, which is set to draw millions of visitors from around the globe.

The Ebola outbreak has already killed more than 200 people in Congo and has been described by health officials as outpacing available resources. A separate U.S. plan to establish an Ebola quarantine facility in Kenya has faced legal challenges, with a Kenyan court this week blocking the opening of such a facility at a military base.

stories.headline: Scientists Identify Iron-Rich Liver Cells as Likely Source of Pigeons' Magnetic Navigation Ability
stories.summary:
A study published Thursday in the journal Science presents the first comprehensive theory explaining how homing pigeons navigate: specialized immune cells in the liver that store iron from broken-down red blood cells appear to detect Earth's magnetic field, effectively functioning as a biological compass. Researchers at Germany's Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior and the University of Bonn conducted the study, which has implications for the broader scientific understanding of magnetoreception across the animal kingdom.

When scientists temporarily depleted pigeons of those iron-storing liver immune cells and released the birds, the animals were unable to find their way home — a result that strongly implicated the cells in directional sensing. Notably, the magnetic disruption only occurred on overcast days, confirming that pigeons also rely on the sun as a secondary navigational tool and switch between systems depending on conditions.

The findings resolve a nearly century-old scientific mystery. Researchers had previously theorized that magnetic sensing occurred in pigeons' eyes, beaks, or inner ears. The liver — an organ not previously associated with navigation — was an unexpected location, though scientists noted that the immune cells sit near nerve fibers that could relay magnetic signals directly to the brain.

The discovery may also shed light on how other migratory animals, including fish and sea turtles, use magnetic fields to navigate over vast distances. Behavioral ecologist Albert Kao of the University of Massachusetts Boston, who was not involved in the research, said the explanation was surprising but compelling once presented.

stories.headline: Update: Netanyahu Directs IDF to Expand Gaza Control to 70% as Ceasefire Strains
stories.summary:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday he has directed the Israel Defense Forces to extend their control of the Gaza Strip from roughly 60% to 70% of its territory, a move that would further contradict the terms of the October 2025 Trump-brokered ceasefire agreement. Speaking at a conference, Netanyahu said the IDF had already moved from 50% to 60% control and signaled further expansion was the next step toward dismantling Hamas. At least 738 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire took effect, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures the United Nations considers reliable.

The announcement comes as Israel and Hamas remain deadlocked in U.S.-brokered indirect talks over the next phases of a 20-point peace plan. Under the ceasefire's terms, the IDF was to withdraw to a negotiated demarcation line, and subsequent steps would involve Hamas disarming and Israeli forces pulling back. Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz this week reaffirmed a pledge to eliminate all leaders of the October 7, 2023, attack and said a plan for what he called "voluntary emigration" from Gaza would be implemented "at the proper time."

Several Israeli strikes this week killed senior Hamas figures, including newly appointed Hamas military wing commander Mohammed Odeh, along with his wife and two sons, just days after his predecessor was killed. A separate strike on a building in Gaza City killed at least 10 people, including five children, according to local hospitals. The Israeli military said it targeted two Hamas operatives in that strike without publicly naming them.

Far-right members of Netanyahu's coalition, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, have publicly backed what they describe as voluntary Palestinian migration from Gaza — a policy that human rights organizations and the United Nations have characterized as potentially amounting to forced displacement, which constitutes a war crime under international law. The situation places additional pressure on U.S.-led ceasefire diplomacy at a moment when Washington is simultaneously negotiating with Iran.

stories.headline: 'Poison Seller' Who Supplied Toxic Chemicals to Suicide Forums Worldwide Pleads Guilty in Canada
stories.summary:
Kenneth Law, a 60-year-old former chef from Ontario, pleaded guilty Friday to 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada after selling toxic chemicals online to individuals he connected with through suicide forums. The guilty pleas were entered as part of a prosecutorial agreement in which more serious murder charges were withdrawn. Authorities say Law sold approximately 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients in 40 countries, and is linked to the deaths of at least 79 people in the United Kingdom alone.

Families of British victims expressed frustration that Law will not face criminal charges in the UK. The Crown Prosecution Service said extradition was "far from guaranteed" and could have taken years, with a risk that prosecution could have been blocked under double jeopardy principles. A CPS prosecutor stated that a condition of the agreement with Canadian authorities was that Law's sentence must reflect deaths that occurred in England and Wales as a result of substances he supplied.

Law is also linked to the deaths of five people in Scotland and one in Northern Ireland. Families of victims described sons and daughters who struggled with mental health following the COVID-19 pandemic and paid as little as the equivalent of £50 for the lethal substances. One father whose 22-year-old son Thomas died in a hotel in Surrey in 2021 said he had wanted Law to face justice in the UK and is calling on the British government to hold a public inquiry.

The case has drawn attention to the role of online platforms in facilitating access to means of suicide, and to the legal complexities of prosecuting cross-border cases involving internet-based offenses. Victim advocates and families are pressing for stronger international cooperation and tighter regulation of online communities that provide information about suicide methods.

stories.headline: At Least 5 Dead After Bus Fails to Slow for Traffic, Strikes Multiple Vehicles on I-95 in Virginia
stories.summary:
At least five people were killed and dozens hospitalized Friday after a bus failed to slow for traffic on Interstate 95 in Stafford County, Virginia, and collided with six other vehicles, according to state police. All five fatalities were passengers or occupants of vehicles struck by the bus. The incident caused significant disruption on one of the East Coast's most heavily traveled highway corridors.

Authorities have not yet released information on the cause of the crash, the identity of the bus operator, or the number and severity of injuries among those hospitalized. Investigations are ongoing. The section of I-95 affected runs through a densely populated corridor between Washington, D.C., and Richmond, Virginia, and carries heavy commercial and passenger traffic daily.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. and Iran Agree to 60-Day Ceasefire Extension, Awaiting Trump Approval
stories.summary:
U.S. and Iranian negotiators have reached a memorandum of understanding to extend the current ceasefire by 60 days and launch formal negotiations over Iran's nuclear program, U.S. sources confirmed to Fox News on Thursday. The agreement was first reported by Axios and is pending final approval from President Donald Trump before it takes effect.

The development marks a significant diplomatic step in a conflict that has roiled global energy markets, stranded roughly 1,500 ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz, and drawn U.S. military forces into direct exchanges with Iranian assets. The ceasefire extension would provide a framework for structured talks on Iran's nuclear capabilities, though the scope and conditions of those talks remain unspecified.

Supporters of the agreement argue it offers a path to de-escalation and relief for global oil markets that have been under severe strain since Iran closed the strait in the war's early days. Skeptics, including some conservative voices, have questioned whether Tehran can be trusted to honor any such agreement and whether a 60-day pause meaningfully constrains Iran's nuclear ambitions.

The White House had previously called an Iranian draft agreement a 'complete fabrication,' making Thursday's confirmed MOU a notable shift. The story is developing, and Trump's final decision is expected to clarify the terms and timeline for any formal ceasefire extension.

stories.headline: Update: Blue Origin Rocket Explosion Casts Doubt on NASA Moon Plans and Amazon Broadband Rollout
stories.summary:
The explosion of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket at Kennedy Space Center on Wednesday evening has raised serious questions about NASA's lunar ambitions and Amazon's broadband satellite constellation. The 98-meter rocket was destroyed during a routine engine test at Space Launch Complex 36, the only facility in the world capable of launching the New Glenn vehicle. No personnel were injured, but the pad suffered extensive damage including the toppling of a lightning protection tower.

The blast carries significant consequences beyond the immediate setback. NASA had tapped New Glenn to carry the Blue Moon Mark 1 lander to the lunar south pole as early as autumn 2026, the first mission in a planned permanent Moon base program. Analysts say rebuilding and recertifying the launch pad will take months, throwing that timetable into serious doubt. Earlier this week, NASA also awarded Blue Origin a contract worth up to $468 million to deliver lunar rovers ahead of a planned 2028 crewed landing.

The explosion also deepens the competitive gap between Amazon's Leo broadband network and SpaceX's Starlink. The destroyed rocket was to have deployed 48 Leo satellites; Amazon currently has just over 300 satellites in orbit compared to Starlink's more than 10,000. With no operational launch pad, Blue Origin has no near-term path to accelerate that deployment.

Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos said on X that the company would 'rebuild whatever needs rebuilding,' but offered no timeline. The incident underscores the risks of NASA's reliance on a single commercial partner for a cornerstone of its lunar infrastructure strategy.

stories.headline: Former Attorney General Pam Bondi Testifies Before Congress in Epstein Probe
stories.summary:
Former U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi appeared Thursday before the House Oversight Committee for closed-door testimony on the Justice Department's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files. Bondi was formally subpoenaed by committee chairman Rep. James Comer, who cited concerns about possible mismanagement of the investigation and compliance with the Epstein Files Transparency Act, legislation Trump signed mandating public release of unclassified Epstein records.

Bondi's tenure as attorney general was marked by sustained bipartisan controversy over the Epstein files. In February 2025, she claimed on Fox News that a list of Epstein's high-profile clients was 'sitting on my desk,' a statement the DOJ subsequently walked back, saying no such client list existed. The department also faced criticism for failing to properly redact victims' names in released documents. Bondi was removed from her post by Trump in April.

Republican Rep. Nancy Mace had accused the Justice Department of a 'cover-up' in its handling of the files, while Democrats simultaneously criticized Bondi for allegedly weaponizing the department against Trump's political adversaries. The committee separately noted that Bondi had served on Trump's 2020 impeachment defense team, adding a layer of political complexity to her role as the nation's top law enforcement officer.

Bondi, who recently disclosed she underwent surgery for thyroid cancer, is set to join the White House's Presidential Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. Transcripts or video of Thursday's testimony may be released publicly at a later date.

stories.headline: Update: Kenyan Court Blocks Opening of U.S. Ebola Quarantine Facility at Military Base
stories.summary:
A Kenyan court on Friday issued a temporary restraining order blocking the opening of a U.S.-run Ebola quarantine center at Laikipia Air Base, roughly 124 miles from Nairobi. The facility, which had been scheduled to open Friday, was designed to hold up to 50 Americans exposed to Ebola while evacuating from the Democratic Republic of Congo, where an active outbreak is ongoing. The court acted on a petition filed by the Katiba Institute, a Kenyan rights organization.

The court order bars authorities from establishing 'any Ebola exposure, quarantine, isolation or treatment facility in Kenya' pending further review. The Kenyan government has 48 hours to respond to the petition. The Katiba Institute argued the center was being established in secrecy and without adequate public process, raising what it called 'grave constitutional concerns.' Kenya's medical workers' union also condemned the move, accusing the government of trading citizens' safety for foreign aid.

U.S. officials said the facility was intended for asymptomatic individuals who may have been exposed to Ebola and that, as of Thursday, no exposed Americans were known to require transport to the center. The Trump administration had framed the facility as a means of providing high-quality care while avoiding the risks of a lengthy journey back to the United States. Kenya had signed a health cooperation agreement with the U.S. in December 2024, though that agreement is also under separate legal challenge.

The ruling adds a new complication to U.S. efforts to manage Ebola risk as the Congo outbreak continues to outpace the global response. Kenya has not reported any Ebola cases from the current outbreak but has been conducting arrival screenings.

stories.headline: Dallas Apartment Building Destroyed in Gas Explosion and Fire; Fatalities Confirmed, Search Ongoing
stories.summary:
An explosion ripped through a two-story apartment complex in Dallas's Oak Cliff neighborhood on Thursday, engulfing the building in flames and sending debris flying into surrounding homes. Dallas Fire-Rescue confirmed there were fatalities but declined to give a specific number while recovery operations continued. Dozens of firefighters searched through smoldering rubble hours after the blaze was brought under control.

Authorities said firefighters were responding to a reported gas leak when the explosion occurred before they could intervene. Natural gas provider Atmos Energy stated that a construction crew unrelated to the company had damaged a pipeline near the site. The company shut off gas service to the area and deployed investigators.

Officials established a family reunification center at a nearby high school as residents reported being unable to reach friends and family members who lived in the building. The mission formally shifted from rescue to recovery. The full death toll and number of residents displaced remained unclear as of Thursday evening.

stories.headline: Update: Hezbollah Deploys Fiber-Optic Drones Against Israel as Casualties Mount During Ceasefire
stories.summary:
Fiber-optic drones have become Hezbollah's primary offensive weapon against Israeli soldiers and civilians along the Lebanese border, six weeks into a ceasefire that took effect in April. The Alma Research Center, an Israeli think tank, has recorded more than 100 drone attacks against Israeli communities since the ceasefire began. One Israeli soldier was killed and two others wounded in a strike near the border community of Shomera on Wednesday; eight of the 11 Israeli soldiers killed during the ceasefire period have died in fiber-optic drone attacks.

Unlike conventional rockets or radio-controlled drones, fiber-optic first-person-view drones fly low, carry explosives, and are guided by a thin optical wire that cannot be jammed by Israel's military systems. The tactic was adapted from the war in Ukraine, where similar weapons have proven highly effective. Residents in frontier communities report little warning before strikes, in stark contrast to the 15-second alert time provided by rocket sirens.

Israeli forces are currently occupying a large section of southern Lebanon under the terms of the ceasefire agreement, and the ongoing drone campaign is increasing pressure on both communities and the military. The development represents a significant escalation in Hezbollah's capabilities and poses a new challenge for Israeli air-defense planners.

stories.headline: Update: Eight Students Arrested in Kenya Over Arson Attack That Killed 16 Girls at Boarding School
stories.summary:
Kenyan police have arrested eight students suspected of planning and executing the arson attack at Utumishi Girls Academy in Gilgil that killed 16 pupils early Thursday. Investigators identified the suspects through interviews with students and staff and a review of CCTV footage, according to the National Police Service. The students were traced to their homes and returned to the school for questioning.

The fire tore through the upper floor of a dormitory housing 135 bunk beds in the early morning hours. Investigations into the precise cause of the blaze are continuing. Distraught parents and relatives gathered outside the school, many still waiting hours later to learn whether their children were among the dead, injured, or arrested.

Kenya has a documented history of deadly school dormitory fires, many attributed to arson by students protesting living conditions or school discipline. Overcrowding and failure to comply with fire safety regulations — including keeping exits clear and windows unlocked — have repeatedly been cited as factors amplifying casualties. At least 21 people died in a similar dormitory fire two years ago.
